strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP need: affordable, compact language models for five major Indian languages. The reported release of models, tokenizers, and instruction datasets, including 5,000 human-authored Bangla examples, offers a potentially useful community resource.

The experimental coverage is substantial, including numerous multilingual and language-specific baselines, individual benchmark results, instruction-tuning comparisons, and ablations of cleaning, tokenization, and context length.

Some reported improvements are meaningful: instruction tuning raises Belebele accuracy from 25.11 to 32.45 for Bangla and from 26.22 to 42.78 for Hindi. These results support further investigation of small monolingual models despite the concerns below.
weaknesses: The memory-saving justification for positional interpolation is technically incorrect as described (§3.5). Replacing token positions with pL/y changes RoPE angles but does not reduce sequence length, activation sizes, or attention computation. It therefore cannot by itself accommodate sequences exceeding a hardware memory limit. The formula also follows the cited positional-interpolation approach, without establishing a distinct contribution. Table 5 varies context length and interpolation together; comparisons with ordinary RoPE at the same sequence length and training budget, including measured memory and runtime, are needed.

Numerical inconsistencies affect the conclusions. In Table 10, the six Hindi-instruct task scores average 38.49, whereas 40.14 is reported and propagated into Table 3. Correcting this reverses its comparison with Llama-3.2-3B at 40.06 and reduces the claimed instruction-tuning gain. Telugu base performance is 32.22 in Tables 3/13 but 32.95 in Tables 4/5. These discrepancies require reconciliation against the underlying evaluation outputs.

The hybrid tokenizer is insufficiently specified and validated (§3.3). Standard SentencePiece BPE does not acquire Viterbi decoding simply by appending Unigram pieces; the description mixes deterministic BPE merging with probabilistic vocabulary search without defining the actual algorithm or score calibration. Vocabulary sizes are omitted. Unigram-only and vocabulary-size-matched BPE controls are needed to distinguish morphological benefits from increased vocabulary capacity. Selected segmentation examples and low fertility alone do not establish morphological alignment.

Many results are close to chance, making uncertainty particularly important. Bangla base averages 25.22 on predominantly four-choice tasks, and Sanskrit-to-Hindi averages 31.05 against an approximate chance macro-average of 30.56 for that task mixture. Without confidence intervals, paired comparisons, or variability estimates for the ablations, small numerical advantages do not establish robust superiority or strong cross-lingual transfer. Exact prompts, answer-scoring conventions, and truncation settings are also needed to assess the comparisons.

Training and instruction-data descriptions are inconsistent enough to impede reproduction. Table 16 implies 26.21B training tokens for Tamil and Telugu, while Table 3 reports 39.32B; the Hindi configuration implies 78.64B rather than 66B. Section 3.4 describes 23K instructions, whereas Appendix C.1 reports 27K for Bangla and Hindi plus 52K additional Hindi Alpaca examples. These distinctions also matter when interpreting differences in instruction-tuning gains. The paper needs reconciled configurations, dataset versions, and a complete instruction-tuning recipe.

Several broader conclusions exceed the evidence. Establishing monolingual training as the 'optimal strategy' requires controlled comparisons with multilingual training or adaptation under matched resource budgets. Translation and retrieval suitability are asserted without evaluating either task. The explanation of Hindi transfer using Marathi versus Hindi perplexities is also unsupported without demonstrating evaluation on the same text with comparable normalization across tokenizers.

The human evaluation (§C.3) uses only ten prompts and an unexplained selection of 'top-3 responses.' Prompt sampling, response selection, decoding settings, blinding, and uncertainty are not sufficiently documented. High annotator agreement cannot compensate for limited prompt coverage or establish broad generation quality. Together with the methodological and reporting issues above, this prevents a sound Findings recommendation at present; a corrected and more carefully scoped submission could reasonably be reconsidered next cycle.
